lessons.title: Context: 1981 Britain, Race & the Care System
lessons.description: Thatcher’s Britain, the 1981 Handsworth riots, and the institutional racism of the care system that shapes Leon’s story.
lessons.content_html:
Britain in 1981

My Name is Leon by Kit de Waal is set in 1981 Birmingham, during a period of intense social upheaval. Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government had been in power since 1979, implementing policies of economic austerity that hit working-class and Black communities hardest. Unemployment was soaring, particularly in industrial cities like Birmingham, and racial tensions were at breaking point.

Key Fact

The novel is set against the real Handsworth riots of July 1981 — sparked by aggressive policing, racial discrimination, and mass unemployment in Black communities.

The sus laws (the ‘suspected person’ laws) allowed police to stop and search anyone they suspected of criminal intent. In practice, this meant young Black men were routinely harassed. The Brixton riots erupted in April 1981, followed by Handsworth in July — both fuelled by the same toxic combination of poverty, racism, and police brutality.

Race Relations in 1980s Britain

The 1980s was a decade when overt racism was commonplace and largely unchallenged by institutions. The National Front had marched openly through cities in the late 1970s. Black and mixed-race families faced discrimination in housing, employment, education, and — crucially for this novel — the care system.

In the 1980s, the care system operated with what we would now recognise as institutional racism. White babies were considered more ‘adoptable’ because there were more white families seeking to adopt. Black and mixed-race children were often left in long-term foster care rather than placed with permanent families.

De Waal draws on real social work practices of the era. The separation of Leon and Jake in the novel reflects documented cases where siblings of different races were split up because the system prioritised racial matching — or, more accurately, prioritised finding homes for white children while failing Black ones.

The care system at this time was also underfunded, with overworked social workers managing enormous caseloads. Children’s emotional needs were often secondary to bureaucratic processes.

The Handsworth Riots

On 10 July 1981, tensions in Handsworth, Birmingham, exploded into violence. Police had conducted aggressive raids on Black-owned businesses and homes. Young people fought back. Cars were burned, shops were looted, and over 100 people were arrested. The riots lasted two days and caused widespread damage.

Key Fact

De Waal uses the riots not just as a backdrop but as a turning point in the plot. They represent the moment when suppressed rage — both communal and personal — finally erupts. Leon’s anger at losing Jake mirrors the community’s anger at systemic injustice.

De Waal wrote this novel in 2016, looking back at 1981. This retrospective viewpoint allows her to show readers how structural racism operated — things that were invisible to many white people at the time are made starkly visible through Leon’s child perspective. The reader can see what Leon cannot fully understand: that the system is not merely failing him, but is designed in ways that disadvantage him because of his race.

Understanding the historical context is essential for literary analysis. When De Waal describes social workers making decisions about Leon and Jake, she is not just telling a fictional story — she is dramatising a real pattern of discrimination that affected thousands of real children.

Kit de Waal’s Background

Kit de Waal (born 1960) grew up in Birmingham as the daughter of an Irish mother and a Kittitian (Caribbean) father. She worked for fifteen years as a magistrates’ court adviser and in criminal law, specialising in cases involving children in care. Her professional experience gives the novel its unflinching accuracy about how the care system operates — and fails.

De Waal has spoken openly about how the novel draws on both her professional knowledge and her personal experience of growing up mixed-race in 1970s and 1980s Britain. The dedication reads: “For all the brothers and sisters who were separated.” This signals that the story, while fictional, represents a widespread reality.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about context, always link it to the writer’s methods and purpose. Don’t just describe what 1981 was like — explain why De Waal chose this setting and how it shapes meaning. For example: “De Waal sets the novel during the Handsworth riots to draw a parallel between Leon’s personal anger and the community’s collective rage against institutional racism.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The novel is set in 1981 Birmingham during a period of mass unemployment, racial tension, and the Handsworth riots.
  • The care system of the 1980s was institutionally racist — white babies were prioritised for adoption while Black and mixed-race children were left in long-term foster care.
  • De Waal draws on her professional experience in family law to create an authentic portrayal of how the system separates siblings.

lessons.title: Part 1: Leon, Jake & Carol
lessons.description: Nine-year-old Leon cares for baby Jake while their mother Carol spirals, setting the stage for the brothers’ separation.
lessons.content_html:
The Opening: Life with Carol

The novel opens with nine-year-old Leon living with his mother Carol and baby half-brother Jake. Leon is mixed-race — his father is Black and absent, his mother is white. Jake is fully white, fathered by a different man. From the first pages, De Waal establishes Leon as a young carer — he feeds Jake, changes nappies, and shields the baby from Carol’s increasingly erratic behaviour.

Key Fact

De Waal uses Leon’s child perspective to show neglect without naming it. Leon doesn’t understand that his mother is struggling with mental health and substance issues — he simply adapts, taking on adult responsibilities because no one else will.

Carol is not presented as a villain. De Waal shows her as a woman overwhelmed by poverty, isolation, and untreated mental health problems. She loves her children but cannot care for them. Her decline is shown through Leon’s eyes: unwashed dishes, curtains drawn all day, Carol sleeping while Jake cries. The reader understands what Leon cannot — that this household is heading toward crisis.

Leon’s Fierce Protection of Jake

The central relationship in Part 1 is between Leon and Jake. Leon’s love for his brother is absolute and physical — he holds Jake, whispers to him, makes him laugh. De Waal establishes this bond so powerfully that its later destruction carries enormous emotional weight.

Physical closeness: Leon is constantly holding, carrying, or lying beside Jake. De Waal uses tactile language — “warm,” “soft,” “tucked in” — to show love expressed through touch rather than words.

Responsibility: Leon takes on a parental role. He knows Jake’s feeding schedule, recognises different cries, and instinctively prioritises Jake’s needs above his own.

Promises: Leon repeatedly promises Jake that he will look after him. These promises become tragic as the narrative progresses and Leon loses the power to keep them.

Leon’s identity: Being Jake’s brother is central to who Leon is. Without Jake, Leon loses his sense of purpose and belonging.

Carol’s Deterioration

De Waal charts Carol’s decline through a series of increasingly alarming scenes, all filtered through Leon’s limited understanding. Carol stops cooking. She sleeps for days. She brings home men who frighten Leon. She disappears, leaving the children alone. The prose becomes fragmented and anxious, mirroring Leon’s growing fear.

Key Fact

De Waal never explicitly states Carol’s diagnosis. Instead, she shows the effects of mental illness and substance abuse through a child’s confused perspective. This technique creates dramatic irony — the reader sees what Leon cannot.

The dramatic irony is central to De Waal’s method. When Leon describes Carol being “tired” or having “medicine,” the adult reader recognises depression, substance use, or both. This gap between Leon’s innocent narration and the reader’s understanding generates both empathy and anguish.

Social Services Intervene

The crisis point arrives when Carol is found unable to care for the children. Social services intervene. Leon and Jake are taken into care together — initially to a temporary placement. Leon is told this is temporary, that he will go home soon. De Waal shows how the system speaks in reassuring language that masks permanent decisions being made behind closed doors.

De Waal contrasts the warm, physical language of Leon’s inner world with the cold, bureaucratic language of social workers. Words like “placement,” “contact,” and “permanency” are used by adults to describe devastating changes in Leon’s life. He doesn’t understand these words, but the reader does.

This contrast highlights the power imbalance between Leon and the adults who control his fate. He has no voice in the decisions being made about him. The child’s perspective forces the reader to experience this powerlessness directly.

Part 1 ends with the brothers still together but the reader sensing that separation is coming. De Waal builds suspense through small, ominous details: social workers whispering, meetings Leon isn’t told about, adults exchanging looks over his head.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing Part 1, focus on De Waal’s use of the child narrator as a method. The gap between what Leon understands and what the reader understands is the source of the novel’s emotional power. Always link this technique to effect: “De Waal uses Leon’s limited perspective to generate pathos because the reader can see the approaching separation that Leon cannot.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Part 1 establishes Leon as a young carer who protects Jake while Carol’s mental health deteriorates.
  • De Waal uses dramatic irony — the reader understands neglect and illness that Leon cannot name.
  • The bond between Leon and Jake is established as the emotional core that the novel will later destroy.

lessons.title: Part 2: Foster Care & Maureen
lessons.description: Leon and Jake are separated by the care system. Leon is placed with foster carer Maureen while Jake is adopted by a white family.
lessons.content_html:
Separation: The System Divides

Part 2 opens with the event that defines the rest of the novel: Leon and Jake are separated. Jake — white, a baby, and therefore ‘more adoptable’ in the language of the system — is placed with a middle-class adoptive family. Leon is placed with foster carer Maureen. The separation is presented as a bureaucratic decision, made in an office, without Leon’s consent or understanding.

Key Fact

Jake is adopted quickly because he is white and a baby — the two characteristics that made children most ‘placeable’ in the 1980s care system. Leon is older, mixed-race, and emotionally damaged. The system sees Jake as an easy success and Leon as a difficult case.

De Waal presents the separation without melodrama. Leon is simply told, in careful language, that Jake is going to live with another family. He doesn’t fully understand that this is permanent. The restraint of the prose makes the scene more devastating — Leon’s silence and confusion speak louder than tears would.

Maureen: Warmth and Stability

Maureen is a Jamaican-British woman who has fostered many children. She is warm, practical, and loving — the opposite of the cold institutional world Leon has just experienced. Her home smells of cooking. She feeds Leon properly. She calls him “sweetheart.” She represents the diaspora community — people who understand racial identity and cultural belonging in ways the white care system does not.

Sensory language: Maureen’s home is presented through warmth, food, and colour. De Waal uses the semantic field of nourishment — both physical and emotional — to contrast with the deprivation of Leon’s previous life.

Cultural identity: Maureen gives Leon something the system cannot — a connection to his Black heritage. She cooks Caribbean food, uses Jamaican dialect, and normalises his mixed-race identity in ways that no social worker has done.

Patience: Maureen doesn’t push Leon to talk or perform gratitude. She allows him space to grieve. Her parenting style is instinctive and community-based, contrasting with the social workers’ procedural approach.

Limitations: Despite her warmth, Maureen cannot fix the fundamental problem — Leon wants Jake, and she cannot give him that. This creates an ongoing tension: Leon loves Maureen but cannot let go of his brother.

Leon’s Internal Conflict

Part 2 is dominated by Leon’s struggle between two impulses: settling into Maureen’s home and refusing to accept the loss of Jake. He begins to form attachments — to Maureen, to the garden, to routines — but guilt pulls him back. Accepting Maureen feels like betraying Jake and Carol.

Key Fact

De Waal presents Leon’s internal conflict through behaviour rather than explicit thought. He acts out, tests boundaries, and oscillates between warmth and withdrawal. His anger is never fully explained to other characters because he lacks the vocabulary to articulate his grief.

Leon’s behaviour in Part 2 includes stealing, lying, and occasional violence. De Waal never presents these as moral failings. Instead, they are shown as the logical responses of a traumatised child trying to regain control over a world that has taken everything from him. The reader is positioned to understand what the system might label as ‘difficult behaviour’ is actually trauma response.

Maureen’s garden becomes a central symbol in Part 2. Leon works in the garden, planting seeds and watching things grow. The garden represents nurture, patience, and the possibility of putting down roots. It offers Leon a form of agency — he can care for something and see results.

However, the garden is also temporary. Leon knows he is in foster care, not adopted. Everything he plants could be taken away, just as Jake was taken. De Waal uses the garden to explore the tension between hope and impermanence that defines the foster care experience.

Contact Visits and Diminishing Hope

Leon is allowed contact visits with Jake, but these become less frequent over time. Each visit is both joyful and agonising — Leon sees Jake changing, growing, becoming part of another family. The visits are supervised, timed, and controlled by adults. Leon has no power over when he sees his brother or for how long.

De Waal uses the diminishing visits structurally: as the gaps between contact grow longer, the reader feels Leon’s grip on his brother loosening. The system is slowly, bureaucratically erasing the sibling bond — not through cruelty, but through process.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Maureen, avoid simplistic readings that position her as a ‘perfect’ mother figure. A top-band answer will explore the limitations of what Maureen can offer — she provides love and cultural identity, but cannot reunite the brothers. Analyse how De Waal uses Maureen to critique the system: even excellent foster care cannot undo the harm of forced separation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jake is adopted because he is white and a baby; Leon is fostered because the system sees him as harder to place.
  • Maureen provides love, stability, and cultural identity, but cannot replace Leon’s lost family.
  • Part 2 explores Leon’s internal conflict between settling with Maureen and refusing to let go of Jake.

lessons.title: Part 3: The Riots & the Ending
lessons.description: The Handsworth riots erupt as Leon’s search for Jake reaches its climax, weaving personal grief with collective anger.
lessons.content_html:
Building Toward the Riots

Part 3 intensifies both the personal and political strands of the novel. Leon is now settled at Maureen’s but consumed by his mission to find Jake. Meanwhile, the streets of Handsworth are crackling with tension. De Waal juxtaposes Leon’s private grief with the community’s collective anger, building toward the moment when both erupt simultaneously.

Key Fact

De Waal uses the riots as a structural parallel: just as the community has been pushed to breaking point by racism and poverty, Leon has been pushed to breaking point by the loss of his brother. Both erupt at the same moment — personal rage and political rage become one.

The build-up to the riots is woven through Part 3 in fragments: conversations Leon overhears between adults, a heightened police presence, neighbours boarding up windows. Leon doesn’t fully understand what is happening politically, but he absorbs the atmosphere of fear and anger. De Waal uses this technique to maintain the child’s-eye view while still communicating the historical context.

Leon’s Search for Jake

Leon’s attempts to find Jake intensify in Part 3. He becomes more resolute and resourceful, gathering information, memorising addresses, and planning how to reach his brother. This quest drives the plot forward and provides the novel with its momentum. It also highlights the absurdity of the situation: a nine-year-old is fighting an entire institutional system alone.

Dual timelines: The personal narrative (Leon searching for Jake) and the political narrative (community tension building toward riots) run in parallel, converging at the climax.

Shortened chapters: De Waal uses shorter, more urgent sections as the novel approaches its climax. Prose becomes punchier, sentences shorter.

Sensory escalation: Sound, heat, and smell intensify — sirens, burning, shouting. Leon’s inner world mirrors the external chaos.

Restricted information: Leon doesn’t understand everything happening around him, which creates tension for the reader who recognises the danger he is walking into.

The Riots: Climax

The climax arrives when the Handsworth riots explode. Leon is out on the streets during the violence. De Waal places him physically in the chaos — fire, breaking glass, running figures, police charges. This is both terrifying and liberating for Leon. The external destruction mirrors his internal world: everything he has suppressed finally detonates.

Key Fact

The riots function on two levels: literally, as a historical event Leon lives through; and symbolically, as the moment when suppressed rage — both personal and communal — breaks through the surface of everyday life.

During the riots, Leon experiences a moment of epiphany. Surrounded by destruction, he understands something about his own anger — that it is not just about Jake, but about a whole system that sees him as less valuable because of his skin colour. The personal and the political fuse. De Waal does not spell this out explicitly; instead, she shows Leon’s perception shifting through imagery and sensory detail.

The Ending: Resolution and Ambiguity

The novel’s ending is deliberately ambiguous. De Waal does not provide a neat, happy conclusion. Leon does not get Jake back in a simple reunion. Instead, the ending offers a more complex form of hope: Leon has survived, he has Maureen, he has a sense of identity, and there is the suggestion — but not the certainty — of future contact with Jake.

Optimistic reading: Leon has found stability with Maureen, developed a stronger sense of identity, and shown extraordinary resilience. The suggestion of future contact means hope is not dead.

Pessimistic reading: The system has won. Jake is permanently separated. Leon has had to accept an outcome he never chose. The damage is done — no amount of love from Maureen can replace a brother.

Critical reading: De Waal refuses a happy ending because real life doesn’t offer one for most care-experienced children. A neat reunion would be dishonest. The ambiguity is the point — it leaves the reader with the discomfort that the system leaves its children with.

De Waal’s choice of ending serves her political purpose. If Leon got Jake back easily, the novel would suggest the system is ultimately fair. By refusing neat resolution, De Waal forces the reader to sit with the injustice — to leave the novel angry, as Leon is angry, as the community is angry.

Structural Significance of the Ending

The novel’s structure is significant: it moves from domesticity (Part 1) through institutional separation (Part 2) to social explosion (Part 3). This mirrors the pattern of oppression itself — private suffering exists silently until it becomes impossible to contain, then erupts publicly. De Waal suggests that what happens to children in care is not separate from what happens on the streets during riots; they are connected expressions of the same systemic failures.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When discussing the ending, always consider multiple interpretations. Strong analytical writing acknowledges ambiguity rather than forcing a single reading. You might write: “De Waal’s refusal to provide neat resolution can be read as both an act of realism and a political statement — the discomfort the reader feels mirrors the ongoing injustice experienced by care-leavers.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The riots function as both historical backdrop and symbolic parallel to Leon’s personal rage.
  • De Waal builds tension through dual timelines, shortened sections, and sensory escalation.
  • The ambiguous ending is a deliberate choice — refusing neat resolution forces the reader to confront ongoing injustice.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Leon’s resilience and loyalty, Maureen’s quiet strength, Carol’s fragility, and how De Waal uses each character to expose the care system.
lessons.content_html:
Leon: Resilience and Loyalty

Leon is nine years old, mixed-race, and the novel’s focaliser. Everything the reader knows is filtered through his understanding. He is defined by two qualities above all: fierce loyalty to Jake, and extraordinary resilience in the face of a system that repeatedly fails him.

Key Fact

Leon’s loyalty and resilience exist in tension. His loyalty drives him to fight for Jake — which the system labels as ‘difficult behaviour.’ His resilience allows him to survive, but surviving means gradually accepting a life without his brother. De Waal shows that the qualities the system punishes (determination, anger) are the same qualities keeping Leon alive.

Leon’s naïveté is crucial to De Waal’s method. He does not understand racism, class, mental illness, or institutional failure as concepts. He simply experiences their effects. This makes him a powerful vehicle for social criticism because the reader can see what Leon cannot, creating both empathy and outrage.

Part 1: Leon is a protector — defined entirely by his relationship to Jake and Carol. He is capable, resourceful, and unnervingly adult in his caring responsibilities.

Part 2: Separated from Jake, Leon struggles with identity. His behaviour deteriorates as grief and anger find no productive outlet. He oscillates between accepting Maureen’s love and rejecting it out of guilt.

Part 3: Leon becomes more defiant and purposeful. His quest for Jake gives him direction. During the riots, he experiences a fusion of personal and political anger that matures his understanding. By the ending, he has not ‘healed’ — but he has survived, which is itself an act of resistance.

Jake: Innocence and Loss

Jake is a baby — he has no voice, no agency, and no understanding of what is happening to him. He functions in the novel primarily as an emblem of what Leon is fighting to keep. Jake represents innocence, family, and everything the system takes from Leon.

Crucially, Jake’s whiteness makes him visible to the system in ways Leon is not. He is adopted by a middle-class family who can provide material comfort but not the sibling bond that Leon offers. De Waal uses Jake to expose the care system’s racial hierarchy: a white baby is a ‘success story’ for adoption statistics, while a mixed-race older child is a ‘difficult placement.’

Carol: Failed by Everyone

Carol is Leon and Jake’s mother. She is white, working-class, and struggling with mental health problems and substance issues. De Waal refuses to demonise her. Carol is not a bad mother — she is a woman without support, without resources, and without adequate mental health services. Her decline is the result of systemic failure, not personal wickedness.

Key Fact

De Waal presents Carol through Leon’s eyes — and Leon loves her. He remembers good times, moments of affection, her smell. This prevents the reader from writing Carol off as simply ‘a bad parent.’ The novel asks: who failed Carol? Where were the services, the community, the father figures?

Carol connects to themes of class, poverty, and gender. She is a single mother in Thatcher’s Britain, where welfare services are being cut. Her absent partners (both Leon’s father and Jake’s) face no consequences, while Carol bears all the responsibility and all the blame.

De Waal uses Carol to critique a system that punishes mothers for poverty rather than providing support. The care system intervenes to remove children but does nothing to address the causes of Carol’s collapse — her isolation, her untreated illness, her lack of financial stability.

Maureen: The Foster Mother

Maureen is Jamaican-British, warm, patient, and experienced. She represents an alternative model of care — community-based, culturally aware, and rooted in love rather than procedure. Her home is sensory: food, music, colour, conversation. She provides Leon with stability, cultural identity, and the first genuine safety he has known.

However, Maureen is not idealised. She has limitations — she cannot reunite Leon with Jake, she cannot undo his trauma, and she must navigate the same institutional system that failed him. De Waal uses Maureen to show that individual love, however powerful, cannot compensate for systemic injustice.

Tina: The Social Worker

Tina represents the institutional system. She is not cruel — she is overworked, bound by policy, and making decisions within a framework that was never designed to serve children like Leon. De Waal presents Tina with nuance — she cares, but her caring is constrained by caseloads, budgets, and rules she did not create.

Tina’s language is significant: she uses euphemisms and bureaucratic terms that obscure what is really happening. “Permanency planning” means Leon will never go home. “Contact arrangements” means limited, supervised visits that will eventually stop. De Waal shows how institutional language can be a form of violence — removing clarity from children who deserve honesty.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about characters, always link characterisation to the writer’s purpose. Don’t just describe what a character is like — explain why De Waal made them that way. For example: “De Waal presents Tina without villainy to show that institutional racism does not require individual racist actors — it operates through structures and processes that even well-meaning people uphold.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Leon is defined by loyalty to Jake and resilience — the same traits the system labels as ‘difficult.’
  • Carol is a victim of systemic failure (poverty, absent services) rather than a villain.
  • Maureen provides love and cultural identity but cannot compensate for institutional injustice.
  • Tina illustrates how institutional racism operates through well-meaning individuals following flawed systems.

lessons.title: Structure, Narration & Voice
lessons.description: How De Waal’s third-person limited perspective through a child’s eyes creates dramatic irony and emotional power.
lessons.content_html:
Narrative Voice: The Child’s Perspective

De Waal tells the entire novel through Leon’s third-person limited perspective. We see, hear, and understand only what Leon does. This is the novel’s most powerful structural choice because it creates a systematic gap between what happens and what is understood.

Key Fact

The child’s perspective forces the reader into an active role. We must interpret what Leon cannot. When he describes Carol ‘sleeping all day’ or ‘smelling funny,’ the reader recognises depression or substance use. This gap generates both empathy (for Leon’s confusion) and anger (at a system he cannot fight because he cannot name what is happening).

De Waal chose third person rather than first person (‘I’). This provides slight narrative distance — enough for the reader to see around Leon, to notice things he misses. A first-person narrator would lock us entirely inside Leon’s head; third-person limited lets us understand his world while also seeing its larger patterns.

Language Register: Simple and Sensory

The prose style mirrors Leon’s age and understanding. Sentences are often short. Vocabulary is concrete and physical. De Waal uses sensory language — touch, smell, taste — rather than abstract thought. Leon experiences the world through his body: the warmth of Jake against his chest, the smell of Maureen’s cooking, the cold of institutional corridors.

Short sentences: Create urgency, mirror a child’s thought patterns, and convey emotional intensity without elaboration. “He holds Jake. He won’t let go.”

Concrete nouns: Leon’s world is built from objects, not ideas — bottles, blankets, gardens, doors. Abstract concepts (racism, institutional failure) are experienced as physical realities.

Present tense sections: De Waal shifts into present tense at moments of high emotional intensity, creating immediacy and drawing the reader into Leon’s present-moment experience.

Minimal dialogue tags: Conversations are often presented without ‘he said,’ creating a sense of voices happening around Leon — sometimes over his head, sometimes directed at him with no context.

Structure: Three Parts

The novel is structured in three distinct parts, each representing a phase of Leon’s experience and a widening of the novel’s scope from domestic to political:

Key Fact

Part 1 (Domestic): Leon, Jake, and Carol at home. Intimate, claustrophobic. Part 2 (Institutional): Separation, foster care, diminishing contact. The system takes centre stage. Part 3 (Political): The riots, Leon’s quest, the personal-political fusion. The scope expands to the whole community.

This three-part structure mirrors a process of radicalisation: from private suffering (Part 1) through institutional betrayal (Part 2) to political awakening (Part 3). De Waal suggests that personal injustice and political injustice are not separate phenomena — one leads to the other.

Temporal Structure: Non-Linear Elements

While the novel is broadly chronological, De Waal incorporates flashbacks and memory fragments that disrupt the forward movement. Leon remembers moments with Carol, with Jake as a newborn, with his absent father. These memories intrude on the present, showing that Leon’s past is never truly past — it inhabits his current reality.

Slow pacing in Part 1: Time passes in domestic rhythms — feeding, sleeping, waiting. This mirrors the monotony and trapped quality of Leon’s home life.

Ellipsis in Part 2: De Waal skips time between contact visits, creating gaps that mirror the growing distance between Leon and Jake. What is omitted is as important as what is shown.

Acceleration in Part 3: Events compress. Chapters shorten. The prose becomes more urgent. This structural acceleration drives toward the climactic riot scenes.

Memory intrusions: Flashbacks arrive without warning, often triggered by sensory details (a smell, a sound). They show Leon’s inability to separate past from present — a hallmark of childhood trauma.

Silence and What Is Not Said

One of De Waal’s most distinctive techniques is the use of omission. Things are not said directly. Leon’s race is rarely stated explicitly — it is shown through how others respond to him. Carol’s diagnosis is never named. The adults’ decisions are made off-page. This technique trusts the reader and mirrors Leon’s experience of not being told what is happening in his own life.

The silences in the text are structurally significant. When Leon stops mentioning Jake for stretches of Part 2, the reader feels the suppression of grief. When Carol disappears from the narrative, her absence speaks louder than her presence did. De Waal uses what is not written as deliberately as what is.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing structure and narrative voice, use precise terminology. Rather than saying ‘it’s written in third person,’ say ‘De Waal uses third-person limited focalised through Leon.’ Rather than ‘it gets faster,’ say ‘De Waal uses structural acceleration through compressed chapters.’ Precise language about form earns higher marks because it demonstrates critical understanding of the writer’s craft.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The third-person limited perspective creates a systematic gap between Leon’s understanding and the reader’s, generating empathy and outrage.
  • The three-part structure mirrors a journey from private suffering to political awakening.
  • De Waal uses omission, silence, and sensory language as deliberate structural choices that reflect the child’s experience of powerlessness.

lessons.title: Key Themes
lessons.description: Structural racism, the care system, family bonds, and belonging — the novel’s central themes and how they interweave.
lessons.content_html:
Theme 1: Racism and the Care System

The novel’s central theme is structural racism — specifically, how racist outcomes can be produced by systems that do not see themselves as racist. The care system does not explicitly state that white babies are worth more than mixed-race children. But its processes, priorities, and outcomes reveal exactly that hierarchy.

Key Fact

De Waal shows racism as structural rather than individual. No single character says anything overtly racist. Instead, racism operates through processes: who is considered ‘adoptable,’ whose needs are prioritised, whose family bonds are valued. This is more insidious — and harder to challenge — than individual prejudice.

The separation of Leon and Jake is the novel’s sharpest critique. Jake is adopted because the system has white families waiting for white babies. Leon is fostered because the system lacks equivalent demand for mixed-race older children. Neither social worker is personally racist — but the outcome is racist. De Waal forces the reader to confront how bias can be built into institutions.

Racism in the novel extends beyond the care system. Leon encounters it in school, on the streets, and in the wider community. The social hierarchies of 1981 Birmingham place Black and mixed-race people at the bottom, denied equal access to housing, employment, and justice.

The Handsworth riots represent the community’s collective refusal to accept this position any longer. De Waal connects the personal (Leon’s separation from Jake) to the political (a community rising against structural oppression) to show that individual suffering and collective injustice have the same root cause.

Theme 2: Family and Separation

De Waal interrogates what ‘family’ means through multiple models: the birth family (Carol, Leon, Jake), the foster family (Maureen), the adoptive family (Jake’s new parents), and the wider community. The novel argues that bonds are created through love and presence, not biology alone — but also that severing existing bonds causes permanent damage.

Key Fact

The novel’s most powerful argument is that sibling bonds matter. The system treats Jake’s placement as a success — he has a stable, affluent home. But it ignores the severed connection to Leon. De Waal suggests that material provision is not the same as emotional wholeness, and that the system’s definition of ‘best interests’ is dangerously narrow.

Theme 3: Identity and Belonging

Leon’s identity is fractured by the system. He is mixed-race in a society that sees race in binary terms. He belongs to a white mother and a Black community. He is neither fully one thing nor another — and the system has no category for this complexity.

Maureen provides cultural anchoring that the care system cannot. Through her, Leon gains access to Caribbean food, music, language, and community. This gives him a sense of belonging that the white institutional world has denied. De Waal suggests that identity is not innate but constructed through relationships and cultural immersion.

De Waal makes identity political. In 1981, mixed-race children in care were often placed with white families who could not help them develop a positive racial identity. The result was children who felt they belonged nowhere. Maureen’s role in the novel is partly a corrective to this — showing what culturally competent care looks like.

Leon’s name is itself significant. The title, My Name is Leon, is a statement of selfhood — a refusal to be reduced to a case number, a ‘placement,’ or a category. By insisting on his name, Leon insists on his individual humanity within a dehumanising system.

Theme 4: Childhood, Neglect and Innocence

The novel explores how neglect robs children of childhood. Leon should be playing, learning, and being carefree. Instead, he is feeding a baby, navigating social workers, and searching for his brother. De Waal shows that poverty and parental illness force children into premature adulthood — not because children are incapable, but because they should not have to be capable.

Yet Leon retains elements of childhood throughout: his love of the garden, his concrete thinking, his inability to grasp abstract concepts like ‘permanency.’ De Waal preserves his innocence even as the world strips it away. This tension between what Leon should be (a child) and what he is forced to become (a carer, a fighter, a survivor) generates the novel’s emotional power.

Theme 5: Class and Poverty

Class operates alongside race throughout the novel. Carol is working-class, unemployed, and without support networks. Jake’s adoptive family is middle-class and comfortable. The care system implicitly values material provision over emotional bonds — a middle-class home with two parents and a garden is deemed ‘better’ than a loving sibling relationship in a poorer setting.

De Waal shows how multiple forms of disadvantage intersect. Carol is disadvantaged by class (working-class), gender (single mother bearing sole responsibility), and circumstance (mental health, absent partners). Leon is disadvantaged by race (mixed-race), age (too old to be easily adopted), and family background (mother in crisis).

The novel argues that these disadvantages are not accidental but systemic. Thatcher’s Britain created conditions where working-class families were more likely to break down and Black children were more likely to be failed by the resulting care system. Individual suffering is connected to political choices.

Theme 6: The 1981 Riots — Resistance and Voice

The riots are not presented as mindless violence but as a form of political resistance. The community has been silenced, policed, and impoverished. The riot is the moment when that silence breaks. De Waal draws a direct parallel: just as Leon has been silenced by a system that does not listen to children, the Black community has been silenced by a state that does not listen to its citizens.

The novel suggests that when legitimate channels fail — when complaints are ignored, when the system does not change — eruption is inevitable. This applies to both the community (rioting) and Leon (acting out). De Waal does not condone violence, but she refuses to condemn it without acknowledging its causes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about themes, never treat them in isolation. The strongest analytical writing shows how themes interconnect. For example: “De Waal interweaves racism and class to show that Leon’s separation from Jake is not caused by one factor alone but by the intersection of racial bias, poverty, and institutional indifference.” Demonstrating thematic connections shows sophisticated understanding.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Racism in the novel is structural — operating through systems and processes rather than individual hatred.
  • Family is defined by love and bonds, not biology — but severing bonds causes permanent harm.
  • The riots represent communal resistance that parallels Leon’s personal refusal to accept injustice.
  • Themes of race, class, gender, and childhood intersect throughout the novel.
